headlines.title: Teen faces murder charges in Fairfield Halloween store mass shooting
headlines.description: A 17-year-old Solano County teen is facing murder and attempted murder charges following a deadly mass shooting last Friday night at a Fairfield Halloween store. The 17-year-old suspect was arrested Monday at his family’s Suisun City home. A spokesperson for the Fairfield Police Department said it did not take long to identify the suspected shooter. “After reviewing surveillance footage from the store, the school resource officer recognized the suspect as a former student and provided that information to the detectives,” said Michelle Belyea of the Fairfield Police Department. Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall said the teenager had an ongoing dispute with one of the six other victims who were wounded in the mass shooting at the Spirit Halloween store located at the Solano Town Center Mall. Marshall also noted that the teen suspect was previously released from a juvenile detention center after serving just a few months for a shooting in a high school parking lot in 2025, though nobody was injured in that crime. Voicing his frustration over the repeat offense, Chief Marshall asked, “How many more people need to get shot or killed before we start making some changes? We need to hold kids accountable.” The big question at this hour is whether the teenage suspect will face these murder and attempted murder charges as a juvenile or be prosecuted as an adult and face life in prison. Steven Clark, a Bay Area legal analyst, said it is very likely the Solano County District Attorney’s Office is considering charging the teen as an adult, though a judge will have the final say. “If this goes to adult court, this young man could be facing the rest of his life in jail. If it stays in juvenile court, he’s likely to be released in his mid-twenties,” Clark said. Constance Hages, a 31-year-old pregnant mother of four, was killed in the shooting. Her aunt posted on Facebook that the family is grieving and trying to raise money through a GoFundMe page to help support her niece’s children and pay for “homegoing” services. Clark added that the judge deciding whether the teen will be tried as an adult will likely listen to victim and family statements before making a final decision. “…and obviously, the most important factor will be the severity of this crime. Certainly, the victim impact statements, to the court, will be very moving and telling, and I think it will be difficult for the court not to move this case to adult court,” Clark said. NBC Bay Area reached out to the Solano County District Attorney’s Office for further comment regarding charges and motives, but they have not yet responded.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. headlines.title: Election Day: Here's what's at stake in the Bay Area as voters head to polls
headlines.description: Bay Area polls are open and voting is underway Tuesday for the November midterm election. California voters will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. From allocating funds aimed at boosting affordable housing to levying a tax on billionaires in the state, voters will also weigh in on 14 California propositions. Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2 There are also a host of key races in the Bay Area. The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Alameda County voters will choose between California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez for who will serve the Congressional District 14’s next full two-year term. Oakland residents will also have their say on whether Barbara Lee will continue to serve as mayor. In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. San Francisco voters are considering several propositions, including Prop B, which would pave the way for a public bank, and Prop G, which would reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Prop H if passed would establish a parcel tax to fund Muni. City voters will also weigh in on the Congressional District 11 race, where Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. In San Mateo County, Measure E in Redwood City would limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay would block proposed farmworker housing and Measure U aims to create an independent commission to draw supervisor districts in the county. In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. South Bay residents will also vote in mayoral races held in Milpitas, Morgan Hill and Santa Clara. Marin County County voters will decide on several measures related to paramedic and emergency medical services. City council seats are also up for election in Novato, San Rafael, Larkspur and Sausalito. In Solano County, voters will choose between Mike Silva and John Carli, who will face in a runoff for a supervisors district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E if passed by voters would establish a tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. Sonoma County voters will decide whether Mike McGuire or James Gallagher takes a seat redistricted by Proposition 50.

headlines.title: Trump and affordability loom over California governor's race between Becerra and Hilton
headlines.description: President Donald Trump, California’s notoriously high cost of living and political experience are on the ballot as voters decide Tuesday whether to elect Democrat Xavier Becerra or Republican Steve Hilton as the next governor of the nation’s most populous state. The winner will succeed Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who can’t seek a third term but is considering a White House run. Becerra, a former state attorney general, has promised to reaffirm California’s status as a liberal counterweight to the Trump administration’s Republican policies. Hilton, a former political adviser in the United Kingdom and Fox News host, has pitched himself as a fresh face ready to set the state back on track after 15 years of Democratic leadership. Hilton faces steep odds. Democrats make up roughly 45% of registered voters in California, compared to Republicans’ 25%. Mail voting has been underway for nearly a month. The Trump administration has sought to sow distrust in the state’s election system by alleging up to 20,000 noncitizens could be registered to vote. The Department of Justice has sued the state in an attempt to stop officials from counting any ballots cast by those people. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s demand on Monday after several lower courts also sided with California. State and local election officials say they follow federal law and the federal government’s numbers are likely inflated. Election experts say voting by noncitizens is rare and has not been shown to change the outcome of elections. Candidates argue over the value of experience Becerra, who also served in Congress and as U.S. health secretary in President Joe Biden’s administration, has argued that he’s best positioned for the job as someone with more than 35 years of experience in politics and government. Hilton has never held elected office. Becerra said at a CNN debate in September that the state needed a leader who could keep the “California dream” alive. “You can’t do it with someone who’s never served, who’s never balanced a budget the size of California, who’s never actually been there to defend people against the tyrant like Donald Trump,” he said. Meanwhile, Hilton has tried to turn his lack of political experience into an asset, arguing the more experienced Democrats who have been in charge have left Californians struggling to afford gas, housing and a college degree. “This is the most amazing state and the most amazing country on Earth, and it’s because we’ve got this rebel spirit,” he said at the debate. “That spirit is being crushed by this bloated, nanny-state bureaucratic government that Xavier has been a part of for 36 years.” A chaotic primary gave way to a low-key general election matchup The two candidates emerged from a large primary field with half a dozen prominent Democrats and two notable Republicans. Becerra wasn’t considered a top contender for the first months of his campaign. That changed when former Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell, who had been viewed as a front-runner, dropped out of the race and resigned from Congress following allegations he sexually assaulted several women. He’s denied the accusations. His departure caused the party establishment and voters to look for a more reliable alternative, and they found one in Becerra. Since then, Becerra has run a relatively low-key campaign, not holding nearly as many public events or press availabilities as Hilton. He’s sought to take advantage of Trump’s deep unpopularity in the state by tying Hilton to Trump, noting the president has endorsed the Republican. Becerra’s campaign launched a website that lists quotes of Hilton expressing support for the president and his policies. The site includes illustrations of the two Republicans standing side by side. Hilton, meanwhile, has tried to break through by releasing splashy ads, sometimes with AI-generated content, to encourage voters who typically choose Democrats to try something new. He’s also tried to appeal to the public by making ambitious promises, including pledging to abolish the DMV and cut gas prices to $3 a gallon, a rate the state hasn’t seen in years. His promise to bring change as a Republican candidate running in California has resonated with some voters. Richard Hartman, an independent voter living outside Sacramento who works in the construction industry, said he was leaning toward voting for Hilton to bring balance to the Democrat-dominated state. He’s particularly concerned about homelessness and the high cost of living. “Nothing works without balance,” he said. “You can’t stand on one leg and walk around. You have to have two feet, and I think that’s the same thing in politics.” Both candidates highlight their families’ immigrant stories For all their differences, Becerra and Hilton share at least one thing in common: Both come from immigrant backgrounds. Hilton’s parents fled communism in Hungary and settled in the United Kingdom, where Hilton was born. Hilton went on to advise former Prime Minister David Cameron before moving to California in 2012. If he wins, he would be the first immigrant to serve as governor since Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger left office in 2011. Becerra was born in Sacramento to a mother from Mexico and a father who was born in California and raised in Mexico. He’s made appealing to Latino voters a key part of his campaign strategy, including by releasing ads and social media posts in Spanish. He’d be the state’s first Latino governor since the late 19th century. His background has appealed to some Californians with Mexican heritage, including Joy Torrez, a Democratic retiree in Sacramento. She proudly planned to vote for him. “I’ve read about him, and I’m really pleased,” Torrez said.

headlines.title: California could become the first state to tax billionaires' wealth
headlines.description: California could become the first state in the nation to tax the net worth of billionaires Tuesday under a ballot measure that has divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history as the ultra-rich scramble to figure out whether they would pay the tax or flee. Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warns it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them. The “no” side has raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who have poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Billionaires are already bracing for its approval. Some of them, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state after the measure was unveiled. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company. Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, say it’s needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years. “It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions. But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition opposing it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents. Californians are divided on the measure. Likely voters were slightly more likely to oppose the measure than support it in a poll conducted in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California, with 52% saying they would vote “no” and 46% saying they would vote “yes.” That’s an apparent shift from a PPIC survey conducted in early September, when 52% of likely voters said they’d vote for the tax and 46% said they’d vote against it. Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it. “Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.” Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.” Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it, which are also on this year’s ballot, passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee has raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin. Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million. Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.” Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said. “We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.

headlines.title: Bay Area transit agencies add service to get fans to Valkyries' parade in San Francisco
headlines.description: Bay Area transit agencies are preparing for large crowds Wednesday as fans head to San Francisco to celebrate the Golden State Valkyries’ historic WNBA championship with a parade at noon. The Valkyries captured their first WNBA championship after defeating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the Finals at Chase Center on Saturday, becoming the first expansion team in the league to win a championship in their second season. Caltrain, BART and SamTrans are encouraging fans to take public transportation to avoid traffic and parking challenges during the celebration. Caltrain will run two additional special trains for the parade. The northbound train 901 will leave San Jose Diridon Station at 9:13 a.m., making all regular stops before reaching San Francisco. After the parade, the southbound train 902 will leave San Francisco Station at 2:40 p.m. and make local stops. Caltrain will also run two afternoon trains as locals to handle crowds. Train 914 will depart San Francisco at 3:10 p.m., followed by train 916 at 3:40 p.m. Riders traveling south of Tamien Station can connect to those trains through services 814 and 816. Fans can walk from Caltrain’s San Francisco station to the parade’s end at 2nd and King streets or head along the Embarcadero toward the starting point at the Ferry Building. Golden State Valkyries Nov 1 Golden State Valkyries Nov 2 Golden State Valkyries Nov 2 BART, meanwhile, will run extra trains, longer trains and add staff and security for the event. Riders can take BART to Embarcadero or Montgomery stations and walk to the parade. Another option is to take BART to Powell Street Station and transfer to Muni’s southbound T Third train at Union Square Station, then get off at 4th and King streets and walk to the parade. SamTrans also offers several routes connecting the Peninsula to downtown San Francisco. Route 292 serves communities in San Mateo County and connects to the Salesforce Transit Center. The FCX and EPX routes also serve the transit center during peak periods. Fans can also take Route 292 or Route ECR to Millbrae Station and transfer to Caltrain for service to San Francisco, SamTrans officials said. The three transit agencies are advising riders to check schedules and real-time updates before leaving.

headlines.title: Testimony slated to start in retrial of Sierra LaMar murder case
headlines.description: Testimony in the retrial of the man accused of killing Morgan Hill teenager Sierra LaMar is expected to start Tuesday. LaMar disappeared on her way to her bus stop before school in 2012. Five years later, Antolin Garcia-Torres was found guilty in her murder, but that decision was later overturned by an appellate court because the district attorney’s office introduced three unrelated kidnapping accusations against him. During opening statements Monday, the Santa Clara County prosecutor tried to paint a picture of the day LaMar disappeared in March 2012. He explained that even though LaMar has not been found, there is evidence connecting LaMar and Garcia-Torres. He said carpet fibers from Garcia-Torres’ car were found on LaMar’s clothing and her DNA and a strand of her hair her found in the trunk. “Sierra’s body has never been found, yet traces of Sierra were found in the car driven by that man right there,” prosecutor O’Bryan Kenney said, pointing at Garcia-Torres. “Traces of that man were found on Sierra‘s clothes. Traces of that man’s car were found on Sierra’s clothes.” Garcia-Torres’ attorney said it was all evidence that was mishandled. “You want to carefully handle the items so that you don’t cross-contaminate or contaminate these items because you’re mishandling the evidence,” defense attorney Al Lopez said. “There’s protocols for this, and you’re going to see they weren’t followed.” Lopez also told the jury that they would be hearing about someone else who could’ve been involved. The trial is expected to resume at 9 a.m. Tuesday and stretch into next year. Morgan Hill Nov 2 Morgan Hill Oct 2 Sierra LaMar murder case: Judge will not recuse himself, jury selection next week

headlines.title: 9 arrested in string of San Jose business burglaries
headlines.description: San Jose police arrested nine people, including three juveniles, on suspicion of burglarizing multiple businesses over the summer, the department announced Monday. The commercial burglaries happened between June 3 and June 24 at three businesses located in the 1600 block of Capitol Avenue, 400 block of Blossom Hill Road, and 1900 block of Camden Avenue, according to police. During the burglaries, the suspects allegedly drove a car through the businesses before grabbing miscellaneous items and taking off, police said. Some of the suspects also were responsible for roughly 50 vehicle burglaries that happened on June 27 and June 29 throughout San Jose, police allege. The adult suspects were identified as 19-year-old Isaiah Ochoa, 19-year-old Jocelyn Gonzalez-Landeros, 21-year-old Diego Barron-Mora, 19-year-old Joshuah Villela, 20-year-old Moises Nava and 23-year-old Diego Frias. The juvenile suspects were identified as a 15-year-old boy, a 17-year-old boy and another 17-year-old boy who is now 18, police said. All nine suspects are San Jose residents. Police said automated license plate reader cameras helped them identify the suspects.

headlines.title: 17-year-old arrested in connection with deadly shooting at Solano Town Center in Fairfield
headlines.description: Police have arrested a 17-year-old boy accused of a deadly shooting inside a Fairfield mall that left a pregnant woman dead and six other people wounded. Investigators said the teen was identified within hours after a school resource officer recognized him in surveillance footage from the store. Police body camera and SWAT video captured the suspect’s arrest outside a home in Suisun City. He now faces suspicion of murder and attempted murder charges stemming from Friday night’s shooting at the Solano Town Center. “After reviewing surveillance footage from the store, the school resource officer recognized the suspect as a former student and provided that information to the detectives,” said Michelle Belya, Fairfield Police Department public information officer. Authorities revealed that the teen had previously spent time in juvenile hall last year in connection with a shooting into a car in the parking lot of a local high school. Investigators said that on Friday night, he opened fire inside the Spirit Halloween store, targeting one customer but hitting seven people. “There was obviously some kind of disagreement prior to the situation,” said Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall. One of the victims, 31-year-old Constance Hages, was killed. Police confirmed she was pregnant, and the district attorney will decide whether the teen should face an additional murder charge in connection with the death of her unborn child. Six others were injured, including one person who remains in critical condition while others are stable. The grandmother of one teenage survivor, who was shot in the stomach, spoke anonymously about the tragedy. “You never think sending your child out to a Halloween store that they maybe won’t come back anymore. It’s just unreal,” she said. “You just didn’t ever think of how harmless it could’ve been, something you usually do, and then it turned into a literal nightmare.” Chief Marshall emphasized the urgent need to address youth violence and accountability. “How many more people need to get shot or killed before we start making some changes? We need to hold kids accountable,” Marshall said. Police believe the 17-year-old was the sole shooter, though the investigation remains ongoing to determine if anyone else was involved. headlines.title: Anthropic posts $17B quarterly revenue but losses continue in fresh IPO filing
headlines.description: Anthropic’s quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing released on Monday. The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude chatbot also disclosed that it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that’s due to be spent in the next 12 months. The numbers were released about a week after Anthropic issued its original IPO filing in preparation for what’s expected to be a blockbuster Wall Street debut later this month. The document, like the earlier filing, shows the company’s revenue is growing but — like its AI rivals — profit is still elusive. Anthropic’s revenue grew by 13 times to $33.2 billion for the first nine months of the year, but it reported a net loss of $104 billion, including a charge of $94 billion for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements. On a quarterly basis, Anthropic lost $23.3 billion on revenue of $17 billion. The filing gave no indication of how much the company ultimately expects to raise, or what the shares will be priced at when it goes public. Anthropic has previously said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

headlines.title: Students reportedly overdose at San Jose school Halloween party
headlines.description: A possible drug overdose during an afterschool party at a San Jose school has left many parents concerned and frightened. Multiple sources tell NBC Bay Area the incident occurred Thursday evening when two students had to be hospitalized after suffering an apparent drug overdose at a Sheppard Middle School Halloween party. One source familiar with the case said it was an over-the-counter drug the students took. The school district was not disclosing Monday what drug the teenagers are suspected of taking. District officials said they have launched an investigation. In an email to NBC Bay Area, the superintendent said the district is limited in the specific details it can share and are taking the matter seriously. The superintendent also said the district is working to determine any necessary follow-up actions. Both students involved are seventh graders at Sheppard Middle School. Both students are out of the hospital and recovering at home, according to the superintendent. “This absolutely concerning. We are talking about teens,” said Harsha Ramchandani, a chief medical officer at Bay Area Community Health. Ramchandani is not involved with the Sheppard Middle School teens, but said over-the-counter drugs can cause serious harm if not taken cautiously — drugs like Benadryl and cough medicine, including Tylenol. “That can cause hallucinations, dangerous heart rhythms, seizure, coma, even death,” she said. Ramchandani said an overdose occurs when the body is not able to handle the drugs a person ingests. The doctor said there was a 31% increase in child exposure to Benadryl, according to the CDC. An exposure is when a parent or a school official called the National Poison Control hotline to report a child has come in contact with the drug.
